name: Kira Khan

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for talking with me, Kira. I'm from the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We have no ties to companies, unions, parties or government, and what you say is confidential. What's a normal day at work like for you?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I run a mid-size excavator at a lithium mine, digging the ore and loading the trucks. Ten-hour shifts, and I drive forty minutes each way from town. I was a bank teller for twenty years, then the branch closed because everyone banks on their phone, then I did three years in a call centre until a chatbot took most of those calls. At fifty-five I thought, fine, I'll go where the machines are big and the pay is better.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm still green. My bucket fills are uneven and I scrape the truck trays more than I should, so the trainer, Joe, calls me Bumper. But I love it. On my days off I'm learning to fly the survey drones, because the mine's short of people for that, and I use AI every day to study the manuals.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say, well, I guess the chatbot that took my call centre job was the peak. I'd post something wry about it online, probably with a photo of my excavator. At work I'd say nothing changes, back to digging.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, I'd be a bit surprised. I've been on the wrong end of tech twice, so I'd half expect it to sneak up again some other way. But for me it means a quiet run to sixty-five, which isn't bad.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep getting better on the excavator and finish my drone licence by mid next year. I'd keep using AI daily for study and for our household budget. And I'd keep putting money into a few shares I bought last year, small amounts, about two hundred a month.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm, almost a bit bored by the idea.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What do you use AI for every day?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Everything from the excavator manual to working out why my drone footage is blurry. I also have it quiz me before my tests, because I'm fifty-eight and things don't stick like they used to. It's like having a tutor in my pocket who never gets tired of the same question.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What shares did you buy?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Small stuff, an index fund and a couple of companies that make mining equipment. Sanjay, my husband, does books for small businesses and he talked me into it. It's maybe three thousand dollars all up, so I'm not exactly a tycoon.

S0.say: I'd say the chatbot that took her call centre job must have been the peak, and post something wry online with a photo of her excavator. At work she'd say it's back to digging.
S0.think: She'd be a little surprised, since she's been on the wrong end of technology twice and would expect it to sneak up another way. For her it means a quiet run to sixty-five.
S0.do: Keeps improving on the excavator and finishes her drone licence by mid next year. Keeps using AI daily for study and budgeting and puts about two hundred a month into shares.
S0.feel: Calm, almost bored by the idea.
S0.quote: It's like having a tutor in my pocket who never gets tired of the same question.
S0.fieldNote: Kira has been displaced by technology twice and responded by moving towards the machines, not away. She uses AI as a daily study tool and is building small investments. Her humour about her nickname, Bumper, shows she's relaxed about being a beginner.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many tasks in many jobs. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. But most people still have work, and society has time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's an adjustment, not the end of the world. Learn the new tools, don't wait for someone to rescue you. I'd say that online and at work, though I'd try not to be preachy about it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I think it's good for me, actually. If the mine brings in self-driving excavators, someone has to watch them, map the pit with drones, and tell the machines where to dig. I want to be that person.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask the manager on day one to put me on the automation trial, and I'd finish the drone licence early. I'd use my days off to learn the pit planning software with AI as my tutor. And I'd keep investing a little each month, maybe bump it to three hundred.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm, and quite excited. It's the first time I'd be early instead of late.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You're junior and still scraping truck trays. Would they really put you on the trial?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Maybe not on skill. But the old hands mostly don't want to sit in a room watching screens. I've already got the drone ticket coming, and I'd make sure the manager knows I'm keen.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who would you worry about?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Joe, my trainer. He's been on excavators for thirty years and he's the best there is, but he hates anything with a screen. I'd want to bring him along with me somehow, maybe as the guy who checks what the machines are doing wrong.

S1.say: I'd say it's an adjustment, not the end of the world, and people should learn the new tools rather than wait to be rescued. She'd try not to be preachy about it.
S1.think: She sees steady change as good for her, because someone will have to supervise self-driving excavators and map the pit with drones. She wants to be that person.
S1.do: Asks to join the automation trial on day one and finishes her drone licence early. Learns pit planning software on days off with AI as her tutor and raises her share investing to about three hundred a month.
S1.feel: Calm and quite excited to be early for once.
S1.quote: It's the first time I'd be early instead of late.
S1.fieldNote: Kira sees steady change as a chance to finally be ahead of technology rather than behind it. Her pragmatic centre outlook shows in her focus on personal action over rescue. She worries about her trainer and wants to bring him along.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. With robots it reaches hands-on work too. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say everyone's in the same boat now, so the government and companies have to work something out together, fast. I'm not one for protests, but I'd vote for whoever has a real plan. Online I'd share practical things, like how to stretch your savings.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think even being early doesn't save me if the AI can do the drone work and the planning too. Two years is enough to get my licence and maybe a year of supervising, then I'm done at sixty. And Sanjay's bookkeeping is exactly what AI does well, so we'd both feel it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd still go for the automation team straight away, because a year of that pay is a year of savings. I'd sell the shares if they'd gone up and keep the cash, roughly five months of expenses plus whatever the shares fetch. Sanjay and I would look at downsizing the house in the second year, maybe moving closer to our daughter in the city.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious. Not frozen, but there's a knot in my stomach that wasn't there before.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why sell the shares when you could keep them?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because if robots do everything, the robot companies' shares might go up, sure, but I can't eat a share when the power bill comes. I'd keep a little bit, maybe a thousand, just in case. Sanjay would argue, and he'd probably be right, but cash helps me sleep.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell your daughter?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ring her and say, Mum's thinking of moving closer, don't panic. She'd panic. Then she'd ask if I'd used the AI to plan it, and I'd say of course I had.

S2.say: I'd say everyone's in the same boat, so government and companies have to work something out fast. She'd vote for whoever has a real plan and share practical money tips online.
S2.think: She thinks being early won't save her if AI can do drone work and planning too, leaving her done at sixty. Sanjay's bookkeeping is exposed as well.
S2.do: Joins the automation team straight away to bank a year of good pay. Sells most of her shares to hold cash and, with Sanjay, plans to downsize and move closer to their daughter in the second year.
S2.feel: Anxious, with a new knot in her stomach, but not frozen.
S2.quote: I can't eat a share when the power bill comes.
S2.fieldNote: Even Kira, who embraces change, feels squeezed by a two-year timeline that hits both her and Sanjay. She stays practical, turning to cash, downsizing and family. She votes rather than protests, which fits her centre outlook.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is a fair warning, so use it. I'd tell people at work to get onto training now. I'd say the government should help people over fifty-five, because we're the ones with the least time to retrain.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd be sixty-three, and I think I'd ride it well. A few years supervising the new machines and flying drones, then retire a bit early. It's tight but doable.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd get onto the automation trial in the first year and finish the drone licence. I'd keep investing a little but also build cash up to a year's worth by 2030. I might do drone surveys for farmers on weekends, for a side income, while there's still demand.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, but I'd feel like I'm steering.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why drone surveys for farmers?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: There are a lot of farms around town that need crop maps and fence checks, and not many people with licences. A guy at the pub charges four hundred a job. I could do a few a month and put it all away.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What changes compared with the two-year picture?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I get to choose instead of scramble. With two years, I'd sell things in a hurry and move in a hurry. With five, I could plan the move, keep the house a bit longer, and leave the mine on my terms.

S3.say: I'd say five years is fair warning, so use it, and get onto training now. The government should help people over fifty-five, who have the least time to retrain.
S3.think: At sixty-three by 2031, she thinks she'd do well with a few years supervising machines and flying drones, then retire a little early. It's tight but doable.
S3.do: Joins the automation trial in the first year and finishes her drone licence. Builds cash to a year's worth by 2030 while still investing a little, and does weekend drone surveys for farmers as a side income.
S3.feel: Uneasy, but feeling like she's steering.
S3.quote: I get to choose instead of scramble.
S3.fieldNote: Five years lets her plan rather than react, which moves her from anxious to uneasy. She spots a concrete side business in farm drone surveys. Her pragmatism shows in balancing investing and cash.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is a gift, so nobody has an excuse. I'd post about learning the tools early and I'd help anyone at work who asked. I'd keep it practical.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: For me, it's good. I'd be sixty-eight and long retired. I'd have years of interesting work supervising the machines first.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep doing what I'm doing: excavator, drones, automation trial when it comes. I'd keep investing two or three hundred a month. I'd help my daughter, who works in marketing, think about what parts of her job might last.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm, and genuinely curious.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell your daughter?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say, look at what I did: bank, call centre, mine. Each time I moved towards the machine instead of away. I'd tell her to find the part of her job where she tells the AI what to do, not the part it does for her.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there anything in this one that worries you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My trainer Joe, again. He's fifty-two, so ten years catches him right before retirement. I'd hate for the best excavator man I know to finish his career sweeping the workshop.

S4.say: I'd say ten years is a gift, so nobody has an excuse. She'd post about learning tools early and help anyone at work who asked.
S4.think: For her it's good news: she'd be long retired at sixty-eight. Before that she'd get years of interesting work supervising the machines.
S4.do: Keeps going on the excavator, drones and automation trial, and keeps investing two or three hundred a month. Helps her daughter in marketing work out which parts of her job will last.
S4.quote: Each time I moved towards the machine instead of away.
S4.fieldNote: With ten years Kira is relaxed and focused on helping others, especially her daughter and her trainer. Her life story of moving towards the machine is her guiding idea. Her one worry is for Joe, whose timing is worse than hers.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The two-year one, because there's no time for being early to pay off, and Sanjay's work goes too. What would help is a short bridge, a payment for people over fifty-five until they reach the pension, and cheap training for whatever jobs are left.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You didn't ask whether I'm angry about being pushed out twice. I'm not, really. The bank and the call centre taught me that the job isn't who you are, it's just where you are for now.

headlineQuote: The job isn't who you are, it's just where you are for now.
portrait: Kira Khan is a fifty-eight-year-old former bank teller and call centre worker who now runs an excavator at a lithium mine, after technology pushed her out of two earlier jobs. She uses AI every day to study, is learning to fly survey drones and invests small amounts in shares. She stays calm through the plateau and steady change, seeing the automation trial as her chance to finally be early. AGI in two years makes her anxious because it would hit both her and her husband's bookkeeping, but with five or ten years she feels she's steering and plans a comfortable exit.
biggestWorry: AGI in two years worries her most, because being early wouldn't have time to pay off and her husband's bookkeeping work would go too.
whatWouldHelp: A bridging payment for people over fifty-five until they reach the pension, and cheap training for the jobs that remain.
